title: Development, Evaluation and Control of Drugs

questions.stem: A patient takes acetaminophen tablets bought in the US together with paracetamol tablets bought in Lebanon. How are these two names related?

options.A: Brand name and generic name of the same drug
options.B: Two different drugs of the same class
options.C: USAN and INN of the same drug
options.D: Chemical (IUPAC) name and generic name of the same drug
options.E: INN and proprietary name of the same drug

questions.explanation: Acetaminophen is the US Adopted Name (USAN) and paracetamol is the WHO International Nonproprietary Name (INN); both are generic names for the same drug, so taking both risks a double dose. A: Brand names are Panadol, Tylenol. B: They are one drug. D: The IUPAC name is N-(4-hydroxyphenyl)acetamide. E: Neither is a proprietary (brand) name.
questions.source: Development, Evaluation and Control of Drugs, slides 6–7

questions.stem: Before first-in-human dosing, a candidate drug is tested for whether it blocks the cardiac hERG potassium channel and prolongs the QT interval. Which preclinical task category is this?
questions.explanation: Safety pharmacology tests for hazardous acute effects such as arrhythmias and bronchoconstriction; hERG block is the slide's example. B: Genotoxicity and the maximum non-toxic dose. C: Absorption, distribution, metabolism, excretion in animals. D: Works out the mechanism of a toxic effect already found. E: Large-scale production, stability and formulation.
questions.source: Development, Evaluation and Control of Drugs, slides 15, 17

questions.stem: Of drugs that enter Phase I, at which transition is a drug least likely to move on to the next stage?
questions.explanation: Only ~29% of drugs pass from Phase II to Phase III; Phase II is the first real test of efficacy in patients, and lack of efficacy is the most common reason for failure. A: ~52% move on from Phase I. C: ~58% pass Phase III. D: ~91% of submissions are approved. E: Phase IV happens after approval; it monitors marketed drugs rather than being a development gate.
questions.source: Development, Evaluation and Control of Drugs, slides 24–25

questions.stem: A new anti-inflammatory drug is approved after Phase III trials in about 3,000 patients showed no serious hepatic toxicity. Two years after marketing, spontaneous reports reveal fulminant hepatitis in about 1 in 10,000 users. What best explains why the trials missed this reaction?

options.A: Phase I was done in healthy volunteers rather than patients
options.B: The Phase III trials were not double-blinded
options.C: The placebo response masked the adverse effect
options.D: Preclinical carcinogenicity studies last only two years
options.E: About 30,000 patients must be treated to see even one case

questions.explanation: By the rule of three, detecting a 1-in-10,000 reaction needs ~30,000 treated patients; Phase III enrolls 300–3,000, so such reactions appear only after marketing (pharmacovigilance, Phase IV). A: Phase II and III are in patients, and the problem is size. B: Blinding controls bias; it does not create rare events. C: Placebo response concerns perceived benefit, not hepatitis. D: Carcinogenicity is a separate animal tumor test.
questions.source: Development, Evaluation and Control of Drugs, slides 42–43

questions.stem: The FDA approves a new monoclonal antibody, a biologic never approved before. How long is the marketing exclusivity granted at approval?
questions.explanation: A new biological product receives 12 years of exclusivity. A: New clinical investigation (e.g., new indication). B: New chemical entity (small molecule). C: Orphan drug (<200,000 US patients). E: Patent term, counted from filing, granted by the patent office, not FDA exclusivity.
questions.source: Development, Evaluation and Control of Drugs, slides 46–48

questions.stem: A patent on a lead compound was filed in 2012, and the drug was approved in 2022. Which statement about its US patent protection is correct?

options.A: Up to 5 years may be restored, with at most 14 years left after approval
options.B: It lasts 20 years counted from the date of approval
options.C: It is granted by the FDA at the time of approval
options.D: It can be renewed once for another 20 years
options.E: It is what stops generics from referencing the brand's clinical data

questions.explanation: Patent term restoration can give back part of the time lost in testing and review: no more than 5 years, and no more than 14 years of patent life after approval. B: 20 years, non-renewable, counted from filing. C: Patents come from the USPTO; the FDA grants exclusivity. D: The term is non-renewable. E: That is marketing (data) exclusivity.
questions.source: Development, Evaluation and Control of Drugs, slides 46–47

questions.stem: In 1961, thousands of babies were born with limb defects after their mothers took a sedative in pregnancy. What did the US law passed in response add to drug approval?

options.A: Proof of safety before a drug can be marketed
options.B: A shorter approval route for generic drugs
options.D: User fees in exchange for FDA review deadlines
options.E: Proof of efficacy from controlled trials

questions.explanation: The thalidomide disaster led to the 1962 Kefauver–Harris Amendments: proof of efficacy as well as safety, from controlled trials, plus informed consent. A: 1938 Food, Drug, and Cosmetic Act (after elixir sulfanilamide). B: 1984 Hatch–Waxman Act. C: 2007 FDA Amendments Act. D: 1992 Prescription Drug User Fee Act.
questions.source: Development, Evaluation and Control of Drugs, slide 38

questions.stem: In a randomized, placebo-controlled antidepressant trial, patients do not know which treatment they receive, but the psychiatrists rating their mood do. The drug group shows a larger improvement than expected. Which design change best addresses the most likely bias?

options.A: Randomize the patients to treatment groups
options.E: Enroll healthy volunteers instead of patients

questions.explanation: The trial is single-blind, so observer bias remains (raters see what they expect); double-blinding hides the treatment from both patient and observer. A, B: Already randomized and placebo-controlled. D: Crossover makes each patient his or her own control but does not hide the treatment from the rater. E: Efficacy must be tested in patients; this does not remove observer bias.
questions.source: Development, Evaluation and Control of Drugs, slide 26
